```{r}
# Only run the code when NOT_CRAN is "true" (needs to download the h3

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  eval = identical(tolower(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN")), "true")
)

# Limit threads to avoid a CRAN NOTE
Sys.setenv(OMP_THREAD_LIMIT = 2)

# Quarto spawns a new R subprocess during R CMD build and may not pick up

local({
  r_libs <- Sys.getenv("R_LIBS")

    paths <- unlist(strsplit(r_libs, .Platform$path.sep))
    .libPaths(unique(c(paths, .libPaths())))
  }
})
```

# Getting started

**{duckh3}** provides fast, memory-efficient functions for working with the [H3 hierarchical indexing system](https://h3geo.org/) in R. It wraps the [DuckDB H3 community extension](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/extensions/h3) and integrates with **{duckspatial}**, **{dplyr}** and **{sf}**, so you can index, aggregate and analyse large datasets with DuckDB while staying in your usual R workflow.

H3 divides the globe into hexagonal cells at 16 resolutions (0 to 15). Each cell has a unique 64-bit index, and every cell has one parent at a coarser resolution and several children at finer ones. That makes H3 useful for spatial binning, joins and neighbourhood analysis without needing any geometry at all.

Let's start by loading the packages we need:

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(duckh3)
library(duckspatial)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
```

# Installation

Install the stable release from CRAN:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("duckh3")
```

Or the latest GitHub version:

``` r
pak::pak("Cidree/duckh3")
```

# Setting up a connection

Every {duckh3} function runs inside a DuckDB connection with the `h3` and `spatial` extensions loaded. Before using the package, create the **default connection** with `ddbh3_default_conn()`. It installs and loads the extensions (the first time it downloads them), registers the {duckh3} SQL macros, and stores the connection so other functions can find it:

```{r}
#| label: default-conn
#| message: false

ddbh3_default_conn(threads = 1)
```

The default connection is shared with {duckspatial}, so both packages operate on the same database. If you want a separate database (for example, a file on disk), create your own connection with `ddbh3_create_conn()` and pass it through the `conn` argument:

```{r}
#| label: user-conn
#| message: false

conn <- ddbh3_create_conn(threads = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note}
H3 indexes are unsigned 64-bit integers. {duckh3} connections use `bigint = "integer64"` so these values are never rounded. If you make a connection yourself with `duckdb::dbConnect()`, set `bigint = "integer64"` too, or store indexes as strings.
:::

# Naming conventions

All functions start with `ddbh3_` (*DuckDB H3*), and the name says what they take and what they return:

| Pattern | Description |
|---|---|
| `ddbh3_lonlat_to_*()` | From longitude/latitude columns |
| `ddbh3_points_to_*()` | From spatial point geometries |
| `ddbh3_polygons_to_*()`, `ddbh3_lines_to_*()` | From polygons or lines (polyfill) |
| `ddbh3_h3_to_*()` | From H3 cells to other representations |
| `ddbh3_vertex_to_*()`, `ddbh3_edge_to_*()` | From H3 vertexes and directed edges |
| `ddbh3_get_*()` | Get a property of a cell (resolution, parent, area...) |
| `ddbh3_is_*()` | Check a property of an index (valid, pentagon...) |

The suffix gives the output: `*_to_h3()` returns an H3 index, `*_to_spatial()` returns hexagon geometries, and `*_to_lon()` / `*_to_lat()` return the coordinates of the cell centre.

# From coordinates to H3 cells

H3 does not need spatial data. Any table with longitude and latitude columns is a valid input. {duckh3} ships a small example dataset of 100 points:

```{r}
#| label: load-points

points_tbl <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata/example_pts.csv", package = "duckh3"),
  row.names = 1
)

head(points_tbl)
```

`ddbh3_lonlat_to_h3()` adds a column with the H3 index of the cell that contains each point. Columns are called `lon` and `lat` by default; use the `lon` and `lat` arguments if yours have other names.

```{r}
#| label: lonlat-to-h3

points_h3 <- ddbh3_lonlat_to_h3(points_tbl, resolution = 5)
points_h3
```

The result is a **lazy table**: the query has been defined in DuckDB, but no data has been brought into R. This lets you chain several operations and have DuckDB optimise them together. Use `collect()` (or `dplyr::pull()`, `as.data.frame()`...) when you need the data in memory:

```{r}
#| label: collect

points_h3 |>
  collect() |>
  head()
```

By default indexes are returned as strings (`h3string`). You can request the `UBIGINT` form instead, which is faster and smaller, and convert between both formats at any time:

```{r}
#| label: bigint

points_bigint <- ddbh3_lonlat_to_h3(
  points_tbl,
  resolution = 5,
  new_column = "h3bigint",
  h3_format  = "bigint"
)

points_bigint |>
  ddbh3_bigint_to_strings(h3 = "h3bigint") |>
  select(id, h3bigint, h3string) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(h3bigint = as.character(h3bigint))
```

# Vectorized mode

When you pass a plain character vector instead of a table (and leave `conn = NULL`), {duckh3} works like a regular vectorised R function and returns a vector:

```{r}
#| label: vectorized

cells <- c("85283473fffffff", "8928308280fffff", "not-an-index")

ddbh3_is_h3(cells)

ddbh3_get_resolution(cells[1:2])
```

This is handy for quick checks. Note that numeric vectors are rejected because doubles cannot store every H3 index exactly; use character strings or `bit64::integer64` instead.

# Output types

Functions that return geometries, like `ddbh3_h3_to_spatial()`, return a `duckspatial_df` by default: a lazy table with a geometry column that {duckspatial} functions understand.

```{r}
#| label: to-spatial

hex_ddbs <- ddbh3_h3_to_spatial(points_h3)
class(hex_ddbs)
```

Use `mode = "sf"` to get an `sf` object directly. You can also change the default for the whole session with `duckspatial::ddbs_options(mode = "sf")`.

```{r}
#| label: to-sf

hex_sf <- ddbh3_h3_to_spatial(points_h3, mode = "sf")
hex_sf
```

Finally, any function can write its result to a table in a DuckDB connection with the `name` argument, instead of returning it. Here we store the points in our own connection, then index the table by name:

```{r}
#| label: name

DBI::dbWriteTable(conn, "points", points_tbl)

ddbh3_lonlat_to_h3(
  "points",
  resolution = 7,
  conn       = conn,
  name       = "points_h3"
)

DBI::dbListTables(conn)
```

# Using {duckh3} inside `mutate()`

{duckh3} registers DuckDB **macros** with the same names as the R functions. On lazy tables you can call them directly inside `dplyr::mutate()`, `filter()` or `summarise()`, and {dbplyr} sends them to DuckDB as SQL. This makes long pipelines very concise:

```{r}
#| label: macros

points_lazy <- dplyr::copy_to(
  duckspatial::ddbs_default_conn(),
  points_tbl,
  name = "points_lazy",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

points_lazy |>
  mutate(
    h3       = ddbh3_lonlat_to_h3(lon, lat, 6),
    h3parent = ddbh3_get_parent(h3, 2),
    area_km2 = ddbh3_get_area(h3) / 1e6
  ) |>
  select(id, h3, h3parent, area_km2)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Macros only exist inside DuckDB, so they work on lazy tables (`tbl_duckdb_connection`, `duckspatial_df`), not on regular data frames. For data frames, use the exported R functions.
:::

# Hierarchy

Each H3 cell has one parent at every coarser resolution and many children at every finer resolution. Moving up the hierarchy is a quick way to aggregate data:

```{r}
#| label: parent

points_h3 |>
  ddbh3_get_parent(resolution = 1) |>
  count(h3parent, sort = TRUE)
```

Moving down returns several cells per input. By default the result is unnested (one row per child); use `nested = TRUE` to keep a list column instead:

```{r}
#| label: children

points_h3 |>
  head(1) |>
  ddbh3_get_children(resolution = 6) |>
  select(id, h3string, h3children)
```

`ddbh3_compact()` does the reverse: it replaces each complete set of children with their parent, which is a compact way to store large areas. `ddbh3_uncompact()` expands them back to a single resolution.

# Neighbours and distances

`ddbh3_grid_disk()` returns every cell within `k` steps of a cell (the "k-ring"), one row per neighbour. `ddbh3_grid_distance()` then gives the number of steps between two cells. Combined with `ddbh3_h3_to_spatial()`, we can map how far each neighbour is from the origin:

```{r}
#| label: grid-disk
#| fig-height: 5

disk <- points_h3 |>
  head(1) |>
  ddbh3_grid_disk(k = 3) |>
  ddbh3_grid_distance(h3start = "h3string", h3end = "h3neighbors") |>
  ddbh3_h3_to_spatial(h3 = "h3neighbors", mode = "sf")

plot(
  disk["grid_distance"],
  pal    = hcl.colors(4, "Teal", rev = TRUE),
  border = "white",
  main   = "Grid distance from the origin cell"
)
```

Grid distances can only be computed between cells that are reasonably close; for cells too far apart the result is `NA`.

Cell size varies with latitude, so H3 cells of the same resolution do not all have the same area. `ddbh3_get_area()` measures each cell, and `ddbh3_get_hexagon_area_avg()` gives the average area at a resolution:

```{r}
#| label: area

points_h3 |>
  ddbh3_get_area(unit = "km^2") |>
  summarise(
    min_area  = min(h3area, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_area = mean(h3area, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_area  = max(h3area, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ddbh3_get_hexagon_area_avg(resolution = 5, unit = "km^2")
```

# From polygons to H3 cells

`ddbh3_polygons_to_h3()` and `ddbh3_polygons_to_spatial()` fill polygons with H3 cells (polyfill). They accept `sf` objects, `duckspatial_df` objects or tables in a connection. Here we use the North Carolina counties that ship with {sf}:

```{r}
#| label: polyfill
#| message: false
#| fig-height: 5

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)

nc_subset <- nc[nc$NAME %in% c("Wake", "Durham", "Orange", "Chatham"), ]

nc_hex <- ddbh3_polygons_to_spatial(nc_subset, resolution = 7, mode = "sf")

plot(st_geometry(nc_hex), col = "#0A7EA4", border = "white", lwd = 0.3)
plot(st_geometry(nc_subset), border = "#FF6B35", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
```

The `containment` argument controls which cells are kept: `"overlap"` (default) keeps any cell that touches the polygon, while `"center"` keeps only cells whose centre falls inside it. For lines, use `ddbh3_lines_to_h3()` and `ddbh3_lines_to_spatial()`.

```{r}
#| label: cleanup
#| include: false

duckdb::dbDisconnect(conn)
```

# Learn more

This vignette covered the main building blocks. The [function reference](https://cidree.github.io/duckh3/reference/index.html) lists everything else, grouped by topic: vertexes, directed edges, local IJ coordinates, icosahedron faces and more. For spatial operations on the resulting hexagons (joins, areas, interpolation), see [{duckspatial}](https://cidree.github.io/duckspatial/).
